newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US wants Germany, Japan on Council, silent on others.
newsitem.headline: US wants Germany, Japan on Council, silent on others.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson on Tuesday said Germany and Japan should be permanent members of the U.N. Security Council but did not say whether they should have veto power or what other states might get seats in the powerful 15-member body.
"Permanent seats for Japan and Germany would be a sine qua non. Within those parameters we are willing to be flexible," he told a U.N. group working on reform of the council.

U.N. ambassadors have been working for three years on expanding the council, whose five permanent members -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- were chosen in 1945 because they were victors over Germany and Japan during the Second World War.
To change the composition of the council, the five permanent members and probably two-thirds of the entire U.N. membership would need to approve a change in the U.N. Charter.
But developing countries, many of whom were colonies in 1945, are adamant that they are unrepresented in the council, although choosing representatives among them has proved almost impossible.
At the same time, some conservatives in the U.S. Congress, who might have to ratify a charter change, are opposed to any poor nations becoming permanent members.
Richardson repeated that the Clinton administration did not want any action that would change the obligations or privileges of the current permanent members of the council.
But it was not clear if this meant denying the veto to any additional members or denying permanent membership status to Third World countries.

The entry into the council by Germany and Japan would also help defray some of the peacekeeping costs and help ameliorate the huge U.S. debt to the United Nations. But both countries insist they would demand full rights, including the veto.

Italy has also lobbied hard to prevent any addition to the five permanent members and prefers more rotating seats, with preference given to larger countries. Should Germany join the council, Italy would be the only major European state not to have a permanent seat.
Richardson's statement came a day after Thailand's ambassador, Asda Jayanama, vice president of the group, announced results of an informal poll of more 165 countries he called "the silent majority."

He told the group that most members wanted the council increased to about 26 seats, five more permanent members and five non-permanent members. Richardson made clear the United States did not want more than 20-21 seats.

"Many of these supporters wanted the new five permanent members to come from both developing and industrialised countries, and that there should be no discrimination between present and new permanent members," he said.
Most ambassadors interviewed believed the veto was anachronistic, but acknowledged it was not realistic to expect it would be abolished, the ambassador said.
